meta.title: Who really said "I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Michael Jordan's line traces to his own 1994 book — whose title is literally the second half of it. But the wording and its famous page number don't hold up.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying'?
meta.ogDescription: Jordan's own 1994 book is titled I Can't Accept Not Trying. The line is his — but no readable page pins this exact wording. Here's what's actually documented.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.authorDates: b. 1963 · American basketball player, six-time NBA champion
answer.sourceLine: Jordan put his name to a 1994 HarperSanFrancisco book called I Can’t Accept Not Trying — literally the second half of this sentence — and Wikiquote’s Michael Jordan entry credits the line to it, though it appends a bracketed editorial gloss, ‘[no hard work]’, that LibQuotes reproduces as ‘(no hard work)’. The book’s text is not openly readable, the page number every aggregator repeats cannot exist in a book this short, and shorter variants circulate under the same citation, so we stop at ‘attributed’ rather than claim we have seen the page.

source.excerpt: I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can’t accept not trying.
trail: Wikiquote’s Michael Jordan entry ↗ credits the line to Jordan’s 1994 book — but it prints the sentence as ‘…But I can’t accept not trying [no hard work]’, bundled in one bullet with a second quote and an inline ‘(p. 20, 24)’, which reads as one page each and is perfectly plausible for a short book. The citation beneath the bullet gives ‘p. 129’, which is not. The entry also has no sourced/unsourced split — every Jordan quote sits in one list, so the citation is the only vetting signal there is.
Open Library’s record ↗ puts the book at 36 pages, HarperSanFrancisco, 1994; the Internet Archive’s scan record for the same edition counts 58. The two disagree — but a page 129 exists in neither.
AZQuotes ↗ and LibQuotes ↗ reproduce the wording with the identical ‘p. 129’ — the signature of one citation copied outward rather than several people checking a book.

The Internet Archive holds a 1994 copy ↗ — a scan its own record puts at 58 pages, against Open Library’s 36 — but its text files return an authorisation error and its search-inside endpoint reports the item unavailable. The one check that would settle this — reading the page — was not open to us.
source.excerptNote: No fuller passage could be confirmed. Every sourced citation we found reproduces the line on its own, and the book itself — a short, photograph-led volume that sets Jordan’s sentences as display type — is not openly readable.

author.name: Michael Jordan
author.heading: Who was Michael Jordan?
author.metaLine: Born 1963 · American basketball player and six-time NBA champion
author.bio: Michael Jordan played fifteen NBA seasons between 1984 and 2003, winning six championships with the Chicago Bulls across two three-peats — 1991–93 and 1996–98. By the mid-1990s he was also a publishing brand: Rare Air (1993) and I Can’t Accept Not Trying (1994) were both built with the writer Mark Vancil. That is why so many ‘Jordan quotes’ trace to a short illustrated book rather than to a transcript, a press conference or a locker-room interview.

misattribution.heading: What actually goes wrong with this one
misattribution.intro: Nobody credits this line to the wrong person — Jordan’s name is on the cover of the book it is said to come from. What goes wrong is the wording, the paperwork, and which Jordan quote you are actually holding.

items.why: A shorter form, ‘I can accept failure, but I can’t accept not trying,’ drops the middle clause entirely and is credited to the same 1994 book on Goodreads ↗. Both forms circulate widely; only one can be the sentence on the page.

A third form runs longer, not shorter. Wikiquote ↗ prints the sentence as ‘…But I can’t accept not trying [no hard work]’, and LibQuotes ↗ carries the addition as plain prose, ‘(no hard work)’ — under the identical p. 129 citation. Our headline wording is the version without it.
Wikiquote, AZQuotes ↗ and LibQuotes all point to p. 129 of a book that Open Library ↗ records as 36 pages. The citation is being copied, not consulted.

This gets blended with ‘I’ve missed over 9,000 shots in my career… and that is why I succeed’, which Wikiquote ↗ records only as ‘quoted in’ Nike Culture: The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), p. 49 — a reproduction, not a claim about where the line started. A separate statement with a separate trail.

misattribution.truthLine: The safe statement: the phrase is Jordan’s own — it is the title of his 1994 book ↗, published under his name with Mark Vancil — but nobody has yet shown the exact sentence on an actual page.

context.heading: Why the trail goes fuzzy
lead: Jordan spent the early 1990s becoming a publishing property as well as a player. Rare Air: Michael on Michael (1993) and I Can’t Accept Not Trying (1994) were both assembled with the writer Mark Vancil — short, photograph-led books that turned his talk about fear and preparation into display type.

That format is precisely why the provenance blurs. A sentence set alone on a page in a slim gift book is easy to shorten, re-punctuate and re-cite, and once a single page number entered the quote web every aggregator copied it — including one that cannot exist.
detailsBody: Quote Investigator ↗, the usual court of appeal for lines like this, has never covered it — a site search for the phrase returns nothing. That is not a verdict either way; it means no specialist has done the archival work, so the wording and the page remain open.

The one check that would close the case is mundane: open a physical copy of the 1994 book and read the ‘Fears’ section. Until someone does, ‘attributed’ is the honest label — the attribution is about as strong as an unread source can be, and the wording is still unconfirmed.
context.pull: The title of his own book is the second half of the sentence.

sourcesVerified.claim:
Wikiquote's Michael Jordan entry prints the line, in one bullet with a second quote, as "I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying [no hard work].
Talent wins games, but teamwork and intelligence wins championships. (p. 20, 24)", with the sub-bullet reference Jordan, Michael, I Can't Accept Not Trying (HarperSanFrancisco, 1994), p. 129; it records the '9,000 shots' line separately as 'As quoted in Nike Culture : The Sign of the Swoosh (1998), by Robert Goldman and Stephen Papson, p. 49'. The article's only headings are 'Quotes', 'Quotes about Jordan' and 'External links' — there is no Sourced/Attributed/Misattributed split.
Open Library's record for the 1994 edition gives publisher HarperSanFrancisco, date 1994, 36 pages, ISBN 0062511904 / 9780062511904, LCCN 94179125.

The Internet Archive holds a copy of 'I can't accept not trying: Michael Jordan on the pursuit of excellence' by Michael Jordan with Mark Vancil, HarperSanFrancisco, 1994, first edition, ISBN 0062511904. Its item metadata gives imagecount 58 — i.e. its scan of the same edition runs to 58 pages, against Open Library's 36; neither reaches 129.
AZQuotes reproduces the wording 'I can accept failure, everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying.' attributed to Michael Jordan and cites the 1994 book at p. 129.

LibQuotes reproduces the wording with Wikiquote's bracketed gloss turned into prose — 'I can accept failure. Everyone fails at something. But I can't accept not trying (no hard work).' — and cites Jordan, Michael, I Can't Accept Not Trying (HarperSanFrancisco, 1994), p. 129.
Goodreads carries the shortened variant 'I can accept failure, but I can't accept not trying', attributed to Michael Jordan and to the book I Can't Accept Not Trying.
A Quote Investigator site search for the phrase returns 'Nothing Found' — the site has no article on this quote.

Michael Jordan was born 17 February 1963 in Brooklyn, New York; he played fifteen NBA seasons between 1984 and 2003 for the Chicago Bulls and Washington Wizards, winning six championships with the Bulls (1991, 1992, 1993, 1996, 1997, 1998).
The Internet Archive holds 'Rare air: Michael on Michael' by Michael Jordan with Mark Vancil, photographs by Walter Iooss, published 1993 by Rare Air, Chicago.
